title: Silicon carbide cell array hybrid-bonded to silicon periphery
idea: Build the access transistors and storage junctions in 4H-SiC (Eg 3.26 eV) and hybrid-bond the array to a Si CMOS periphery wafer.
why: Junction generation leakage scales with intrinsic carrier density, which is ~1e-8 cm^-3 in SiC against ~1e10 in Si. That allows refresh-free, hour-scale retention, and SiC substrate supply is expanding in the U.S. through EV demand.

title: Solar PERC passivation: negative-charge AlOx liner around storage junctions
idea: Adapted from the PERC solar cell's field-effect passivation: line the buried-wordline trench and storage-node contact sidewalls with 2-5 nm ALD Al2O3, which carries ~1e12-1e13 cm^-2 fixed negative charge. The charge accumulates holes at the p-type surface, starving interface traps near the storage-node junction of the depletion they need to generate leakage current.
why: Solar makers cut surface recombination 10-100x this way; aimed at the access-device junction it targets the trap-dominated leakage tail (fact 3), plausibly doubling worst-cell retention with one extra ALD step and no EUV.

title: Solar advanced hydrogenation: light-assisted trap passivation of storage junctions
idea: Adapted from the PV industry's advanced hydrogenation, which uses intense illumination during a 200-400 C anneal to shift hydrogen into its mobile, reactive charge state: run it after the access-transistor module so hydrogen reaches and passivates the deep-level defects at the storage-node junction that create the leakage tail.
why: Tail cells are dominated by a few deep traps; passivating them could shrink the 13 fA tail 3-10x (fact 3) with low-cost tools that solar fabs already run at GW scale.

title: Solar-wafer gettering sinks buried under arrays to vacuum up tail metals
idea: Multicrystalline solar silicon became usable through phosphorus-diffusion and cavity gettering that pull Fe, Cu and Ni out of the active volume. Build a sacrificial gettering band 2-3 um under each DRAM array (carbon co-implant plus a hydrogen-implanted cavity layer, no scarce helium) and add a late low-temperature 'gettering soak' so transition-metal deep-level traps migrate away from storage junctions.
why: Retention-tail and VRT cells cluster at metal/defect sites; shrinking the tail 3-10x moves the refresh-limiting cell population and raises yield of 32-64 Gb dies (fact 3).

title: Tea-bag steeping: molecular monolayer doping forms damage-free storage junctions
idea: A tea bag delivers flavor by surface contact, not force. Instead of implanting arsenic/phosphorus (or BF2 for p+), self-assemble a monolayer of phosphorus-bearing molecules such as diethyl vinylphosphonate on the storage-node contact, cap it with oxide and drive it in with a spike anneal, giving ultra-shallow junctions with no implant damage and no fluorine.
why: End-of-range implant defects are prime retention-tail trap sites (fact 3); damage-free junctions could tighten the tail 2-5x.

title: Recombination-enhanced annealing pulses lock VRT defects in benign state
idea: Variable-retention-time cells come from metastable defects that flip between high- and low-generation configurations over a ~0.5-1 eV barrier. Periodically park a row's data in a spare row by in-DRAM copy, then pulse its bitlines ~0.3 V below the p-well for ~1 us to forward-bias the storage junctions, and write the data back. Injected minority carriers recombine at the defect, delivering ~1 eV per event to drive it into its low-leakage configuration (recombination-enhanced defect reaction).
why: VRT forces 2-4x refresh guardbands and makes retention profiling unsafe. Locking defects into the benign state would remove that guardband and make per-row refresh trustworthy (fact 3).

title: Carbon-cluster proximity gettering pulls metal traps from storage junctions
idea: Mid-gap metal impurities (Fe, Cu, Ni at ~1e10 cm^-3) are ideal SRH generation centers, and image sensors remove dark-current hot pixels with buried carbon-cluster gettering layers. Implant a C3H5 molecular cluster layer ~1 um under the array before the well anneals, so metals precipitate there, away from storage-node depletion regions.
why: SRH generation scales with trap density in the depletion region. Cutting metallic traps 10x compresses the leakage tail that sets the 64 ms interval (fact 3), for one implant step and no lithography.

title: Carbon co-implant gettering scrubs iron from storage junctions
idea: Scale shift to ppb impurities: a single mid-gap Fe or Ni atom in a depletion region can create a 1e-9 tail cell, so carbon is implanted a few hundred nm below the array (with an oxygen-precipitate denuded zone) and C-related complexes getter transition metals away from storage junctions throughout the thermal budget.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): tail cells are often single-defect; gettering targets 2-5x fewer tail cells and longer refresh bins using only carbon.

title: Nanosecond laser melt regrows defect-free storage junctions
idea: Effect: liquid-phase epitaxial regrowth. After the storage-node implant, a ~50 ns UV/green laser pulse melts only the top ~20 nm, regrowing the junction epitaxially and dissolving end-of-range dislocation loops that act as generation centres, while the short thermal budget spares buried wordlines. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 2-3x tail compression, translated into internal refresh relaxation.

title: Solid-source phosphorus drive-in grades storage junctions to cut peak field
idea: P: instead of implanting the storage-node junction, fill the self-aligned contact hole with phosphosilicate glass and drive phosphorus in by rapid thermal anneal, forming an implant-damage-free, linearly graded junction with ~30-40% lower peak field and no added mask.
why: Trap-assisted tunnelling leakage rises exponentially with peak junction field (fact 3); a damage-free, low-field junction can cut tail leakage several-fold using only mature, non-EUV steps.

title: Metal impurities rationed to zero: carbon-cluster proximity gettering under storage junctions
idea: Limit: no transition-metal atom may survive within 1 um of a storage junction. Implant carbon-cluster (C3H5) ions to form a gettering layer a few hundred nm beneath the array, the trick CMOS image sensors use against hot pixels. The layer captures Fe, Ni and Cu that would otherwise sit in junction depletion regions as deep-level generation centers.
why: Fact 3: the extreme leakage tail is tied to deep-level metal contaminants. Image sensors cut white-pixel counts ~10x this way; a similar tail compression would allow 2-4x longer refresh.

title: Resonant adiabatic refresh recycles bitline energy through on-die inductors
idea: Worse: dump the full CV2 of every bitline swing to ground on each refresh. Flip: during refresh-only cycles, swing bitline and wordline groups through an on-die LC tank (TSV or RDL spiral inductors) that returns charge between half-mats instead of dissipating it.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) and CV2 floor (fact 10) down 50-70% for refresh cycles.

title: Eliminate resistance: superconducting persistent-current loop cryogenic memory tier
idea: Store each bit as a clockwise or counter-clockwise persistent current in a superconducting NbN loop, accessed through a kinetic-inductance nanowire switch briefly driven normal by a write pulse. A persistent current never decays, so there is no leakage and no refresh; deploy as a 4 K tier beside superconducting or quantum compute.
why: Zero static leakage, fJ-level switching, refresh removed entirely; niobium thin films need no EUV. Density is limited by loop inductance (~1 um^2 cells) and cryo overhead.

title: Persistent-current superconducting loop memory for cryogenic racks
idea: IFR: the bit circulates forever with zero loss. For cryogenic AI racks, store bits as clockwise or counter-clockwise persistent currents in NbN kinetic-inductance nanowire loops switched by nanocryotron gates, with no leakage, no refresh and no static power.
why: Facts 3 and 10: infinite retention and fJ-scale switching; loop area (sub-um^2) limits density, but fits cryo computing where DRAM performs poorly.

title: Hermit crab's borrowed shell: re-screen retired DIMMs at faster refresh
idea: A hermit crab moves into a used shell. Hyperscaler-retired DDR4/DDR5 modules are bulk-tested hot for retention, re-binned, and redeployed behind CXL memory expanders that run them at 2-4x refresh rate with stronger ECC as pooled cold-tier memory.
why: Adds usable memory without new wafers; extra refresh compensates for aged retention tails. Even a few % of the retired fleet is a large supply in a 4x price spike.

title: Space-AI noise training: models learn to ignore 1% weight flips
idea: Satellite AI on commercial hardware is trained with fault injection. Fine-tune LLM and vision models with random 1% bit flips injected into stored weights (with exponent clamping at load), producing weights that run from unrefreshed, ECC-free DRAM at 1% cell BER with negligible accuracy loss.
why: Fact 3 and supply: weights are 50-80% of inference memory; dropping 12.5% ECC and most refresh frees capacity and energy with no hardware change.

title: Deliberately non-uniform mats: tall and short capacitors by data lifetime
idea: Inverts 'all cells must be identical': fabricate two retention classes on one die, tall-capacitor long-retention mats (refresh ~1 s) and short-capacitor no-guarantee mats (1-10 ms) that skip the deepest etch, and expose them as separate NUMA tiers so the OS places long-lived pages and transient buffers where each is cheapest.
why: Splits capacitor cost and refresh cost (facts 1, 3): short mats save process steps and area, long mats cut most refresh energy; ~2x better blended cost-energy.

title: Substitute xenon flash and excimer anneals with microwave activation
idea: Substitute xenon flash-lamp and excimer-laser anneals (both rare-gas tools) with 5.8 GHz microwave annealing below 500 C. The microwaves couple to implant damage and dopants, activating and healing them without diffusing the graded storage-junction profile.
why: Keeps a soft, graded junction that lowers BTBT/GIDL while repairing damage-related generation centers: target 2-5x lower junction leakage from a gas-free tool.

title: Woven memory: crossbar cells where drawn fibers cross in a textile
idea: Inverts 'memory is lithographed on a flat wafer': thermally draw multimaterial fibers (metal core with Schottky-diode shell, or metal core with dielectric shell) down to ~1 um by the kilometre, then weave or align-lay them orthogonally so every crossing is a diode-capacitor cell, and stack woven sheets into blocks.
why: Fiber drawing makes km of device per hour at material cost, so a 100-layer block reaches ~$0.1/GB-class (~100x cheaper); trade-off: low areal density, slow high-capacitance lines, contact variability.

title: Time-to-live allocations: never refresh data that dies first
idea: Time shift from the fixed 64 ms refresh clock to software data lifetimes: allocators (malloc, PyTorch caching allocator, NIC buffers) tag buffers with a TTL, and the memory controller keeps a per-row 'expires-at' timestamp, skipping refresh for rows whose contents will be overwritten or freed before their retention bin runs out and stopping refresh on freed rows entirely.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3): in AI training/inference 50-80% of DRAM bytes are short-lived tensors living <30 ms, so refresh operations drop ~2-4x and refresh's share of idle power falls from ~25% to <10%.

title: Access-scheduled refresh: OS rotates hot pages across every row
idea: Scale jump from DRAM rows to OS page tables and time shift to workload access intervals: the kernel and a controller indirection table periodically re-place frequently touched pages so natural activations sweep every physical row within its retention window, and rows activated recently are logged and skipped by refresh.
why: Refresh ops/bandwidth (fact 3): in bandwidth-heavy AI serving, explicit refresh is cut 40-70%; spreading activations also lowers per-row hammer counts (fact 9).

title: Let cells decay: soft-decision LDPC reads stretched-refresh charge
idea: Time shift: deliberately run refresh at 1-2 s and treat retention loss as a noisy channel; sense amplifiers add a second offset reference so each read also returns a 'weak' flag, and an on-die LDPC decoder uses those soft bits to correct 1e-4-class decay errors, scrubbing rows whose weak-flag count rises.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3): 16-32x fewer refreshes for ~6-10% parity overhead, importing NAND's soft-decision playbook into DRAM timescales.

title: Resonant LC wordline drivers recycle refresh energy
idea: Time shift that exploits refresh's metronome-like periodicity: because refresh activations arrive on a fixed cadence, refresh wordlines and sense-amp enables are driven from an on-package LC tank tuned to that cadence, swinging the ~3 V wordline adiabatically and returning ~60-70% of the CV^2 charge to the tank instead of dumping it from a charge pump.
why: Refresh energy and voltage floor (facts 3, 10): wordline boost pumps are ~30-40% efficient, so adiabatic driving cuts refresh wordline energy ~3x, borrowing resonant clocking from CPUs.

title: Dual-timescale back-gate: deep negative bias only during idle seconds
idea: Time shift between access bursts (ns) and idle stretches (s): build the array on thin-BOX SOI with a per-bank back-gate plane held near 0 V during bursts for strong on-current, then pumped to about -2 V after ~10 us idle, raising access-transistor Vt ~200-300 mV and cutting subthreshold leakage ~100x.
why: Idle refresh power (fact 3): self-refresh interval stretches 10-50x in idle-dominated mobile and server profiles with no access-speed penalty.

title: Compress years of VRT behaviour into minutes at wafer sort
idea: Time shift: accelerate rare variable-retention-time toggling (dwell times of hours at 85 C) with a sort step combining 150 C, cyclic bias-temperature stress on wordlines and a hydrogen-rich ambient, so metastable traps toggle many times within minutes; cells seen toggling are fused out or binned.
why: Refresh guardband (fact 3): VRT is why vendors keep 64 ms though most cells hold seconds; catching VRT cells at test lets field refresh relax 4-8x.

title: Heteroepitaxial 3C-SiC access pillar: retention from milliseconds to hours
idea: Time shift through bandgap: grow the vertical access-channel pillars as 3C-SiC (Si and C only, N/Al dopants) on the Si wafer; SiC's intrinsic carrier density (~1e-1 cm^-3 versus 1e10 for Si) suppresses generation and band-to-band leakage by >10 decades, so retention becomes limited by the capacitor dielectric instead of the transistor.
why: Leakage tail/refresh (fact 3): minutes-to-hours retention removes >99% of refresh; all elements Earth-abundant, no W or Hf in the device.

title: Copper buried wordline with self-forming manganese silicate barrier
idea: Scale shift of a BEOL interconnect trick (um) into the ~10 nm buried-wordline trench, plus a time shift in row cycle: fill with CuMn alloy and anneal so Mn diffuses to the SiO2 liner and forms a ~1 nm self-aligned MnSiOx barrier, replacing TiN/W fill and avoiding TaN; the lower RC shortens every refresh row activation.
why: W chokepoint (China ~80%) plus refresh time (fact 3): ~3x lower wordline resistance trims tRFC/row cycle ~20-30%, recovering refresh bandwidth; risk is Cu diffusion into the channel.

title: Refresh locked to the rhythm of AI training steps
idea: Time shift by synchronizing two clocks: AI accelerators run near-periodic steps (forward, backward, all-reduce) with predictable memory-idle phases; the runtime publishes a phase schedule and the memory controller bunches refresh bursts into compute-bound and all-reduce windows on plain silicon DRAM with no new elements.
why: Refresh bandwidth loss (10-20%, fact 3) is >90% hidden with zero material change; the constraint pushes the gain into timing instead of chemistry.

title: QLC-SSD poly-channel stacking: 3D DRAM tiers on NAND's process
idea: 3D NAND reaches 300+ layers with leaky, variable poly-Si channels because controllers absorb ~1e-2 raw BER. Build vertical-bitline 3D DRAM with poly-Si lateral access devices deposited in the stack, accepting grain-boundary leakage and variability as ~1% raw BER handled by page LDPC.
why: Fact 2: existing NAND fabs (depreciated tool sets, some in the U.S.) could make 3D DRAM tiers without single-crystal Si/SiGe epitaxial stacks, making the ~26-tier break-even reachable.

title: Micro-Williams tube: field-emission beam addresses bare electret film
idea: IFR: no cell has an access device; one beam serves a million bits. Each 30x30 um tile has a gated field-emitter tip and electrostatic deflection plates in a vacuum-sealed MEMS cavity, writing and reading 10-15 nm charge spots on a continuous SiO2/Si3N4 electret film (read by secondary-electron yield, then rewrite).
why: Constraint: the medium is an unpatterned film at ~100-200 nm^2/bit versus 864 nm^2 for 6F^2 at 12 nm, and tiles need only coarse MEMS lithography, targeting 5-10x density at lower cost; electret charge in vacuum lasts years, so no refresh.

title: Ferroelectric deadbolt raises access threshold only during sleep
idea: IFR: lock the door when you leave. A thin ferroelectric in the access-transistor gate stack is flipped once at sleep entry to raise Vt by ~0.5-1 V (deep off, retention of hours) and flipped back at wake, so it cycles once per sleep event (~1e6 lifetime) rather than per access.
why: Fact 3: self-refresh (16-33% of idle power) drops toward zero in sleeping servers and phones without weakening active drive current.

title: Eliminate refresh of unallocated memory: OS free-page refresh mask
idea: The OS page allocator exports a free/zeroed-page bitmap to the memory controller over a CXL or DDR mode-register channel; rows holding only free pages are excluded from refresh and zero-filled on reallocation. Servers commonly leave 20-50% of DRAM unallocated or as droppable clean cache.
why: Removes 20-50% of refresh operations fleet-wide with no cell change, saving idle power and bandwidth at 32-64 Gb densities.

title: BEAMOS revival: electron-beam addressed storage with no access transistor
idea: Revive GE's 1970s BEAMOS: a MEMS-deflected array of molybdenum field-emitter microcolumns (one per ~64k-bit tile, in a vacuum cavity wafer-bonded over the die) writes and reads charge on fully floating MOS storage islands via secondary-emission balance, so no bit is ever tied to a transistor. Refresh becomes a slow background raster sweep, as on a Williams tube.
why: Removes the access transistor and its leakage tail (fact 3); a floating island leaks only through dielectric, so retention could reach hours and refresh energy drop >100x; periphery shrinks to beam drivers (fact 7). Open risk: 10-100 ns spot access with fast deflection.

title: Newspaper-press model ROM: reprint inference weights each release
idea: Store frozen inference weights in via- or imprint-programmed mask ROM printed on mature U.S. nodes, reprinted per model release like a newspaper edition. It is byte-addressable at ~10-20 ns behind the accelerator.
why: Zero refresh: printed vias never leak. It removes the largest read-only consumer of HBM/DRAM capacity at a fraction of the cost per bit, with no EUV.

title: Refresh scan turns uniform rows into a single metadata bit
idea: Reverse refresh from a pure cost into a survey: as the refresh engine senses each row, a small comparator in the sense-amp stripe detects rows that are all-0 or all-1 and sets a bit in a per-subarray bitmap. Those rows drop out of the refresh schedule and their contents are regenerated from the bitmap when next opened.
why: Refresh energy/time (fact 3): zeroed and freed pages are often 20-50% of server DRAM, so refresh energy and idle power fall by a similar share.

title: Aerogel thermal-break trench between accelerator and HBM
idea: Worse: bolt the DRAM onto the hottest chip in the system. Flip: cut a silica-aerogel-filled trench in the interposer between GPU and HBM footprints and give HBM its own top heat-pipe path, holding the stack 20-25 C cooler than the logic die.
why: Leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C, so refresh rate (fact 3) drops ~4x and HBM can drop from 2x to 1x refresh mode.

title: Coaxial cable shielding: grounded TiN sleeve kills passing-wordline leakage
idea: Coax stops signals coupling by wrapping them in a grounded shield. Wrap each buried wordline's passing segment, where it runs beside a neighbor's storage junction, with a thin grounded TiN sleeve deposited from TiCl4/NH3 (fluorine-free), so the passing gate cannot invert or field-stress the neighbor's junction edge.
why: Passing-gate-induced leakage and GIDL in neighbors is a known retention and disturb mechanism at 6F2/4F2 (facts 3, 9); shielding could cut that tail component >5x.

title: Armstrong superregenerative sensing to read deeply decayed cells
idea: Revive Armstrong's 1922 superregenerative receiver: replace the single latch with a quenched regenerative sense stage whose exponential build-up time encodes the initial bitline differential, read by a time-to-digital comparator. It resolves signals 5-10x smaller than today's ~100 mV margin.
why: If sensing works at 10-20% of nominal charge, cells can decay far longer before refresh (fact 3) and a smaller Cs becomes usable (fact 1), giving 3-5x longer refresh intervals.

title: Check bits capped at 3%: Z-channel codes for one-way leakage
idea: Limit: no more ECC overhead than today. Retention errors are unidirectional: charged cells decay, empty cells do not, and polarity is fixed per true or anti cell. Map logical bits to physical polarity, then encode each 512-bit row segment with asymmetric (Z-channel, Varshamov-Tenengolts-style) codes. These correct t one-way errors with far fewer check bits than symmetric BCH.
why: Fact 3: correcting ~2-3x more retention errors at equal overhead permits ~4-8x longer refresh intervals in the exponential-tail regime, a direct cut to refresh energy and bandwidth loss.

title: Vacuum-gap NEMS relay as the leak-free access switch
idea: IFR: the off-switch is empty space. Replace each access transistor with a vertical nanoelectromechanical relay (TiN/Ru beam, ~5 nm sealed vacuum gap) pulled in electrostatically by the wordline; when off there is no conductor between storage node and bitline, and a 1 nm carbon contact coating fights stiction and wear.
why: Fact 3: off-leakage falls from fA to tunneling-limited <1e-21 A, so retention goes from 64 ms to hours and the ~46 fJ/bit refresh plus 10-20% bandwidth tax disappear; contact endurance toward 1e15 cycles is the gamble.

title: Shortened-tRCD reads act as a non-destructive charge gauge
idea: A cell's remaining charge sets how fast its bitline develops, so reading a row with a deliberately shortened tRCD fails first on the cells that have leaked most. The sense amplifier still restores the row correctly. Probe rows this way periodically, then re-read at nominal timing for the real data, to build a live per-row charge-margin map and give each row its own refresh interval. FPGA controller work, ~$250k.
why: Online profiling that preserves data gets around the VRT problem that makes static profiles unsafe, enabling per-row refresh at 2-4x the average interval (fact 3).

title: Reactor surveillance-capsule canary cells that age ahead of the array
idea: Reactor vessels carry test specimens placed to age faster than the vessel itself. Put canary cells in every bank with deliberately weakened isolation (shorter gate, thinner spacer, higher junction field) so they lose data and wear 3-5x faster; the controller sets refresh from when canaries fail, tracking a 30-year industrial life.
why: Fact 3: replaces a worst-case-plus-margin 64 ms schedule with a measured, aging-aware one, typically 2-4x less refresh early in life while staying safe as traps accumulate.

title: Random-wired memory: nanowire mesh with addresses discovered, not designed
idea: Inverts 'every cell has a designed address': spray a random mesh of core-shell nanowires (each a gated-diode storage element) between coarse electrode grids, then let a self-test routine discover which electrode pairs reach a usable cell, store the map in on-chip flash, and address through stochastically doped decoder wires instead of patterned decoders.
why: No overlay or fine litho, so cost tracks coating plus coarse patterning (~100x cheaper per GB claimed), with refresh tuned per discovered cell; trade-off is ~30-60% usable sites and a lookup table.

title: Retention rejects rewired as twin-cell half-density parts
idea: A fuse or metal-option mode pairs each cell with its bitline-pair neighbor storing the complement (2T2C). That doubles the sense signal and extends retention ~10x, so dies that would be scrapped sell at half density.
why: Raises usable supply from yield-loss wafers using only legacy fuse and test tools.

title: Purdue SiC DRAM revival on U.S. SiC wafers for refresh-free tiers
idea: Revive the 1990s Purdue 6H/4H-SiC DRAM cells, which retained charge for hours at room temperature: build 4H-SiC access transistors and storage capacitors on 200 mm SiC wafers grown in North Carolina and processed in New York SiC fabs, accepting ~90 nm-class geometry for a retention tier that almost never refreshes.
why: SiC's 3.3 eV bandgap cuts intrinsic generation leakage by >1e10 versus Si (fact 3), so refresh energy is ~0; the supply chain is all U.S. and needs no EUV (fact 4). Density is lower, so it targets idle or standby capacity.

title: Nanoelectromechanical relay as zero-leakage DRAM access switch
idea: Box: MIM cap x electrostatic NEMS cantilever relay in a sealed gap x charge-share SA x BEOL monolithic over periphery x Si x sacrificial-layer release with Ru contacts. When open the gap carries essentially zero current, so only capacitor-dielectric leakage remains; ~1-10 ns mechanical closure on a 20 nm gap.
why: Removes the access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3): refresh interval set by dielectric leakage (seconds+), and relays need no tight Vt so wordline can drop below 1 V (fact 10). Contact endurance >1e12 is the risk.

title: Cesiated vacuum nano-channel access device: off state is literal vacuum
idea: Cs: form a ~20 nm sealed vacuum gap between a cesium/oxide-coated emitter (work function ~1.5 eV) on the storage node and a bitline collector, with the wordline as gate; field emission turns on exponentially at a few volts, and the off state conducts nothing through solid matter.
why: Removes semiconductor leakage paths entirely (fact 3), leaving retention set by capacitor dielectric; Cs stability, hermetic sealing and emitter variability are the risks.

title: Wide-bandgap memory carve-out funding conversion of U.S. power-device fabs
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: government acts as the intermediary between under-used U.S. SiC/GaN power-electronics lines and hyperscaler demand. A CHIPS-style program co-funds converting 150-200 mm wide-bandgap lines into refresh-free memory pilot lines and backs them with five-year hyperscaler offtake contracts for low-refresh capacity tiers.
why: U.S. manufacturability (1-2% share) and capital intensity: reuses existing tools and cleanrooms instead of $15B greenfield fabs; non-silicon substrates avoid the Spruce Pine quartz-crucible chokepoint.

title: Compiler-certified weight re-reads replace refresh during LLM decoding
idea: Every activation is a full restore, and an LLM decode step streams all weights every ~10-50 ms. Add a pass to an open compiler (TVM, Triton or XLA) that proves each weight row is re-read within 32 ms, reordering layer streams if needed. It hands the memory controller a manifest to drop REF for those banks. A small team can demonstrate it on an FPGA accelerator testbed for under $1M in 18 months.
why: Weights fill 60-80% of inference memory, so suppressing their refresh removes most of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss and its energy (fact 3).

title: Substitute per-word SECDED with row-wide LDPC in sense stripe
idea: Substitute 64-bit Hamming with a 4 KB-row LDPC code: parity sits in spare columns and the decoder in the sense-amp stripe. Tail-cell retention failures become correctable erasures, so tREFI can be set at a ~1e-5 raw bit error rate instead of zero failures.
why: 8-16x longer refresh interval (refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth loss recovered) for ~6% parity overhead.

title: Solar junction-box bypass: power-gate and replace leaky mats in the field
idea: Adapted from the bypass diodes that route current around a shaded or cracked solar cell: each memory mat gets its own power gate and well switch plus a remap entry, so a mat whose leakage rises (seen in its refresh-error rate) is switched fully off and replaced by a spare mat in the same bank.
why: One leaky mat today forces the whole device to refresh faster or be scrapped; mat-level bypass repairs it in the field, removes its standby leakage, and keeps the rest of the die at a relaxed refresh rate (fact 3).

title: Closed-loop refresh servo from DDR5 error-check-and-scrub counters
idea: 10-person constraint: no silicon, only firmware listening to the die. Read DDR5's built-in ECS (error check and scrub) counts and the on-die ECC error reports per bank. A PI controller stretches each bank's refresh interval until the corrected-error rate reaches a set target (e.g. 1e-12 per bit-hour), and backs off as temperature rises.
why: Fact 3: refresh follows actual leakage instead of the worst-case datasheet, typically 2-4x fewer refreshes at the same reliability. It ships as BMC or memory-controller firmware.

title: Leakage becomes the latch: tunnel-diode Goto pair on storage node
idea: Reverse leakage from enemy to keeper: stack two nanoscale Esaki (interband tunnel) diodes in series between VDD and ground with the storage node at their midpoint. Their negative differential resistance creates two stable node voltages held by valley-current tunneling, so the node never drifts and the access transistor is only used to read and write.
why: Refresh disappears (fact 3) if diode valley current is <1 pA (otherwise static power rivals refresh); diodes stack vertically on the node, reviving the old TSRAM idea with modern Ge/Si tunnel junctions.

title: Casparian-strip ring seals storage-node sidewall leakage path
idea: Like the suberin Casparian strip that blocks the apoplastic bypass in plant roots and forces flow through gated membranes, selectively recess the STI sidewall where the storage-node junction meets it and fill a thin ring of low-trap, ultra-wide-gap dielectric (crystalline AlN or ALD Al2O3), cutting the interface trap-assisted path so leakage can only go through the gated channel.
why: The worst cells in the leakage tail are dominated by STI-edge and interface trap-assisted tunneling; removing that path narrows the distribution so worst-case retention improves ~4-8x and refresh rate falls proportionally.

title: Salad-dressing solvent cleans distilled and reused on tool
idea: Random stimulus 'salad dressing': oil and water do not mix, so use the oil. Remove post-etch fluoropolymer residue from wordline and contact etches with hydrofluoroether solvent blends (low surface tension, wets 60:1 trenches without collapse) that are distilled and reused >98% inside the tool, replacing aqueous amine cleans plus DI rinses.
why: Takes aqueous chemistry and rinse water out of the access module's residue cleans (>10x less UPW); low surface tension protects tall pillars and preserves leakage-critical geometry (fact 3).

title: TI TSRAM fixed with atomically exact 2D resonant tunneling diodes
idea: TI's tunneling SRAM added two resonant tunneling diodes to a DRAM storage node to make it static. It died on peak-current spread from monolayer thickness fluctuations in III-V barriers, and on standby current. Use graphene/hBN/graphene RTDs, whose barrier is exactly 2 or 3 atomic layers by construction, with valley current engineered to the pA level.
why: Every 1T1C node becomes a bistable latch, so refresh is eliminated at ~nW/Mb standby while 1T1C density is kept. Attacks refresh energy and the refresh bandwidth tax.

title: Moll-Tarui ferroelectric transistor as a sleep-only Vt shifter
idea: Revive the 1963 Moll-Tarui ferroelectric-gate transistor, but switch it only when entering and leaving long idle: a thin HZO layer, using hafnium refined in Albany, Oregon, sits in the access-transistor gate stack. It is poled to raise Vt ~0.4-0.5 V during self-refresh and re-poled to low Vt on wake, so endurance needs are only ~1e6-1e8 events.
why: A ~0.45 V Vt shift at ~80 mV/decade cuts subthreshold leakage by ~5 decades, so self-refresh intervals can grow 100x or more (then limited by junction and GIDL leakage), cutting the 16-33% idle-power share (fact 3).

title: Make refresh opt-in in the JEDEC standard
idea: Reverse the default in the DRAM standard: define a 'host-guaranteed retention' mode in which the die's internal refresh counter is disabled and the host certifies every row is touched or refreshed within the window, backed by an on-die watchdog bitmap that raises an alert if any row ages out. This standardizes what coverage-based, multi-rate and placement-based controllers need from existing dies.
why: Unlocks 50-90% refresh savings (fact 3) across the installed fab base through a spec revision instead of new process technology.

title: Allocator-driven row refresh: never refresh empty memory
idea: Disable auto-refresh on an FPGA/CXL memory controller and issue targeted ACT-PRE refreshes only for rows backing allocated pages. The kernel's buddy allocator updates the bitmap of allocated rows through a doorbell register. Freed pages are simply abandoned and zeroed on reallocation. Kernel plus controller code costs ~$300k over 12 months.
why: Refresh energy scales with rows refreshed, and fleet memory is often 30-50% free or reclaimable, so about that fraction of refresh energy and REF bandwidth comes back (fact 3).

title: Per-module retention passport in SPD, standardized by JEDEC
idea: IFR: each module is refreshed exactly as fast as it needs, no faster. Testers already measure retention, so JEDEC adds an SPD retention passport (per-bank retention histogram at three temperatures) plus a controller rule that stretches tREFI to match, and vendors sell 128/256/512 ms bins.
why: Fact 3: most dies retain far longer than the 64 ms worst-case spec; fleet-wide refresh power and bandwidth could drop 2-8x with no new silicon.

title: Substitute scrapping retention-fail dies with retention-binned memory SKUs
idea: Substitute pass/fail retention screening with binning. Dies that fail 64 ms at 85 C are sold with an SPD flag for 32 ms refresh or for cooled racks; long-retention dies sell at a premium into low-power edge and mobile.
why: Raises usable bit supply 3-8% from existing wafers with zero capital, and turns retention into a priced feature.

title: Electrocyte-stacked access pair exploits series-stack leakage suppression
idea: Electric eels stack electrocytes in series; build each BEOL access device as two vertically stacked oxide FETs on one wordline, so in the off-state the floating midpoint self-biases, giving the upper FET negative Vgs and reduced Vds, at zero extra footprint because the stack is vertical.
why: The stack effect cuts off-current ~10-30x with a modest on-current penalty, extending refresh interval proportionally in a <=400 C process.

title: Hot-mode twin-cell switch trades half the capacity for 4x retention
idea: Worse at 125 C: keep single-ended cells that fail as the leakage spike eats the signal. Flip: above 110 C the controller remaps selected banks to differential twin-cell mode (a bit and its complement on adjacent cells), doubling signal and cancelling common-mode decay.
why: Retention ~4x and refresh 4x lower in the hot regime (fact 3), with no new device.

title: Compiler tensor liveness wired into per-row refresh skip
idea: The ML compiler already knows every tensor's lifetime. It tags buffers whose last read comes within the guaranteed retention window (activations in the decode loop, gradient staging, temp scratch), and the controller sets per-row no-refresh bits until they are freed.
why: Refresh bandwidth and energy fall in proportion to the ephemeral share of the footprint, often 30-60% in training and inference.

title: Gecko-setae dry transfer of wafer-scale WSe2 access channels
idea: Geckos stick and release with switchable van der Waals adhesion; grow wafer-scale bilayer WSe2 at high temperature on sapphire, pick it up with a gecko-like microfibrillar stamp whose adhesion switches with peel angle, and laminate it onto the BEOL memory layer at room temperature.
why: A 1.3 nm body with ~1.6 eV gap gives near-ideal short-channel control and off-current ~1e-19 A/um, so BEOL access devices hold charge for seconds with no >400 C step on the memory wafer.

title: Atomic aluminate dipole sets threshold, channel left undoped
idea: Scale shift from statistical dopant atoms (~10-20 randomly placed per channel at F=12 nm) to one deterministic atomic sheet: a ~0.3 nm AlOx layer at the gate-dielectric/SiO2 interface forms a dipole shifting nFET Vt by +0.2-0.4 V, so the access channel can be left undoped; lower doping lowers the storage-junction field and collapses the trap-assisted tunnelling and GIDL that form the tail.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): random dopant fluctuation and high junction fields cause the <=13 fA tail; expect a 3-10x tighter tail using only Al and O.

title: Buy retention-reject DRAM and qualify it for cooled datacenters
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: dies binned out for leakage-tail failures at 85 C / 64 ms are not dead, only heat-intolerant. A business buys these rejects, re-screens them at 25-40 C with a 16-32 ms refresh contract, and sells them as qualified modules for immersion- or liquid-cooled racks, with controller firmware enforcing each module's refresh profile.
why: Raises usable supply by recovering a few percent of output from existing fabs with zero new capex; buyers get bits well below 4x contract prices.

title: Astrophotography dark-frame subtraction: sense reference that tracks predicted decay
idea: Astronomers subtract a dark frame because dark current is predictable. Store a 2-bit leakage class per row from test, and lower the sense amplifier's reference (dummy-cell level) with time-since-refresh according to that class, so a partly decayed '1' still resolves against a reference that has 'decayed' alongside it.
why: Reclaims roughly half the sensing margin now spent on decay, giving 2-3x longer refresh intervals (fact 3) with no cell change.

title: Eliminate yield loss from retention: sell short-retention dies to streaming customers
idea: Bin dies that fail 64 ms retention but pass 8-16 ms and sell them at a discount into weight-streaming inference appliances whose firmware runs 4-8x refresh or proves per-pass re-reads. Dies now scrapped or patched with redundancy become supply.
why: Raises usable DRAM bit supply a few percent up to ~10% per wafer during a 4x price shock without new fabs (capital intensity).

title: Octopus-arm local refresh brains in BEOL thin-film logic above mats
idea: Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons sit in its arms; build each mat's refresh controller (row counter, sentinel comparator, hammer integrator) from <=400 C oxide/2D thin-film transistors stacked directly above that mat rather than in the silicon periphery.
why: Moves refresh logic out of the ~49% periphery footprint into otherwise unused BEOL area above the array and shortens refresh wiring, for ~20-30% lower refresh energy and a smaller die.

title: Open BMC retention telemetry builds per-part-number refresh tables
idea: Ship an open-source BMC agent that logs corrected-error addresses, DIMM temperatures and part/lot numbers, and runs a 2-minute monthly retention probe on one drained rank. Pool anonymized data across operators into a public per-lot retention model that publishes safe tREFI tables with quantified risk. Software plus a small data team, <$700k over 24 months.
why: Spec refresh is set by the worst lot of the worst vendor; statistics over 100k+ DIMMs justify 2-4x relaxation for most lots (fact 3).

title: Venus-flytrap analog charge integrator counts row activations
idea: The flytrap counts two touches within ~20 s with a decaying calcium level; give each row group a tiny leaky capacitor in its wordline driver that receives a fixed charge quantum per activation and decays with a ~ms constant, and fire a targeted neighbor refresh when it crosses threshold.
why: Gives per-row aggressor tracking with 1-2 transistors and a capacitor instead of SRAM counter tables, stopping row hammer at ~1k-activation thresholds for ~0.2% area and fewer spurious mitigation refreshes.

title: Delay-line regeneration reborn as a self-timed refresh wave
idea: Mercury delay-line memories died on serial latency, but they refreshed themselves by recirculating every bit through a regenerator. Make refresh a travelling wave in the same way: each subarray refreshes one row locally, then hands a token to its neighbor, so refresh ripples continuously across the die. There are no global REF commands or all-bank stalls; the controller only sees a known 1-of-N subarray busy.
why: Recovers most of the 10-20% of bandwidth lost to refresh at 32-64 Gb and flattens peak refresh current. Scheduling moves on-die with negligible periphery.

title: Self-servoed wordline-low voltage holds off-current constant
idea: Worse at 125 C: keep the wordline-low level fixed while Vt falls ~1 mV/K and leakage soars. Flip: a replica access transistor's measured off-current closes a loop that drives the array wordline-low rail (0 to -0.5 V), holding leakage constant from 25 to 125 C and compensating aging over 10 years.
why: Hot leakage (fact 3) cut 10-30x versus fixed bias; refresh can stay near the 85 C rate at 125 C.

title: Curvature-rounded, ultra-graded storage junction to flatten peak field
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: replace sharp corners with curves. A hydrogen-anneal silicon-migration step rounds the recess-channel corners at the storage-node edge, and a laser-spike-diffused wide graded junction replaces the abrupt one, cutting the peak lateral field from ~1 MV/cm toward ~0.6 MV/cm, where trap-assisted tunnelling depends exponentially on field.
why: Shrinks the TAT/GIDL tail (Fact 3) ~5-10x with existing tool types; low-cost, incremental.

title: LaB6 multi-beam maskless writer prints only the access-gate cut layer
idea: La: deploy a massively parallel e-beam writer (LaB6 source split into ~10^5 beamlets) dedicated to the single cut/contact layer that isolates access transistors and lands storage contacts, while every other layer uses DUV pitch multiplication; no mask set and no EUV scanner are needed.
why: Removes the EUV dependency for the 1-2 layers DUV cannot pitch-split cleanly (fact 4) at a fraction of EUV capital; throughput limits it to a few layers per wafer.

title: Dual-mode Hf-Zr-O capacitor parks idle data as polarization, stopping refresh
idea: Hf: make the storage dielectric an HfZrO stack that behaves as a linear dielectric at DRAM bias but switches ferroelectrically under a higher 'park' voltage; when a page goes idle, the controller writes its data as remanent polarization (no refresh), and on wake restores it to charge mode, using the larger capacitor area a DUV-only cell affords for ample switched charge.
why: Idle-page refresh (16-33% of idle power, fact 3) falls to ~zero while active data keeps DRAM endurance, since fatigue accrues only per park cycle (~10^5/day), not per access.

title: Canal-lock access: series switches with an equalized middle chamber
idea: Adapted from canal locks, which equalize a chamber before opening a gate: put two access transistors in series and drive their middle node with a minimum-size follower whose gate is the storage node, so the inner transistor always sees ~0 V drain-source. Both gates open together for read/write; in hold, the storage-side device has almost no Vds to drive leakage.
why: Subthreshold leakage scales with (1 - exp(-Vds/kT/q)); holding Vds near 0 on the inner device cuts its leakage 10-100x and removes it from the retention tail (fact 3), at the cost of extra vertical transistors that 3D tiers could hide.

title: CAM-photosynthesis refresh banking before predicted traffic bursts
idea: CAM plants fix CO2 at night as malate and keep stomata shut by day; before predicted bandwidth peaks (all-reduce, batch prefill) the controller refreshes rows with a boosted restore level (~1.15-1.2x VARY via extended VPP write), banking extra charge so the bank can skip 2-3 refresh periods during the burst and catch up afterward.
why: Recovers the 10-20% refresh bandwidth exactly when it matters, with no increase in average energy.

title: Pharma cold chain: a refrigerated memory tier near minus 30 C
idea: Adapted from the pharmaceutical cold chain: capacity DIMMs sit in sealed, dry-nitrogen-purged sleds on a separate glycol loop chilled to about -30 C by a shared rack chiller, and the controller scales the refresh interval with measured die temperature.
why: Junction leakage roughly halves every 8-10 C, so going from 85 C to -30 C stretches retention 100-1000x and nearly removes refresh (fact 3); chiller energy is shared across a rack, and wires and transistors also speed up.

title: IBM nanotube logic failure recast as printed foil refresh periphery
idea: IBM's carbon-nanotube transistor program stalled because logic needed perfect tube placement and purity. Printed random networks of semiconducting CNTs make p-type TFTs that tolerate that randomness. Paired with printed n-type oxide TFTs, they form complementary circuits on the foil for per-tile sense amplifiers and refresh/ECC controllers next to the oxide access arrays.
why: Putting refresh periphery on the foil removes silicon companion chips, and CMOS on foil keeps standby power low. Manufacturable roll-to-roll in the U.S.

title: Phone-sleep charge overdrive: boosted restore before self-refresh
idea: Phones spend >90% of their time in standby. When memory enters self-refresh, write back every row once with the array voltage boosted ~1.3x (and wordline boost to pass it), storing ~30% more charge so cells take longer to droop to the sense threshold, then self-refresh at a proportionally slower rate.
why: Fact 3: ~1.5-2x lower self-refresh rate in standby, the phone's biggest DRAM energy term; dielectric stress and higher leakage at high stored voltage limit it to sleep only.

title: On-die retention fingerprint ROM drives per-row refresh skipping
idea: Worse: refresh every row at the rate its single weakest cell demands. Flip: at wafer test bin each row's retention (64/128/256/512 ms) into an on-die antifuse table; the internal refresh counter reads the 2-bit tag and skips 3 of 4 REF slots for the ~99% of rows that hold >256 ms.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3): ~60-75% less refresh energy and bandwidth loss at 32-64 Gb with ~0.1% die area for the table.

title: Reclaim retention-failed dies for short-lived AI buffers
idea: IFR: no die is scrap. Dies that fail 64 ms retention screening are binned by measured retention (8-32 ms) and sold as accelerator scratch modules, where the controller refreshes faster or the runtime guarantees the data (activations, KV spill) dies sooner.
why: Scarcity: recovers a few percent of wafer output with zero capex; at 4x contract prices each recovered percent is worth billions in supply.

title: QLC-flash lesson: two-bit-per-cell DRAM at 1% symbol errors
idea: NAND moved to 4 bits per cell by accepting high raw BER plus strong LDPC. Store four charge levels per DRAM capacitor with a two-step coarse/fine sense amp, refresh when level spacing decays to the 1%-error point, and decode with the page code.
why: Cost per bit: ~2x bits per cell (~1.7x net after parity and slower sensing) without more tiers or EUV layers; refresh rises ~2-3x, offset by the 1%-quantile policy.

title: Junctionless nanosheet access device removes the storage-node p-n junction
idea: Make the access transistor a uniformly n+ (~1e19 cm^-3) 5 nm nanosheet that the wordline workfunction fully depletes when off. Source, channel and storage node are then one doping type, so no reverse-biased metallurgical junction touches the storage node. A buried dielectric, not a p-well, isolates it from the substrate.
why: The dominant tail mechanism, SRH/TAT generation in the storage-junction depletion region, has no junction left to occur in. Negative off-bias controls the remaining subthreshold leakage. Expect ~10x tail compression and a correspondingly longer refresh interval (fact 3).

title: Magnify off-resistance to a vacuum gap: NEMS access relay
idea: Replace the access transistor with a 30 nm torsional nanoelectromechanical contact relay (Ru/RuO2 tip, 3-5 nm sealed vacuum gap) pulled in by the wordline; when open the gap passes essentially zero current, leaving only capacitor dielectric leakage. Hermetic BEOL sealing targets 1e15 contact cycles.
why: Deletes the access-device leakage tail entirely; retention limited by the dielectric (minutes-hours), refresh nearly eliminated; contact endurance is the risk.

title: Solar-cell Al2O3 negative-charge liner passivates isolation sidewalls
idea: Box: standard cap x standard access x SA x in-array x Si x ALD Al2O3 STI liner carrying ~-5e12 cm-2 fixed charge (the PERC solar-cell trick) replacing the oxide liner, zero masks. The negative charge accumulates holes on the trench sidewall next to the storage junction, field-effect passivating edge interface states.
why: STI-edge generation is a known tail source; this passivation cut solar surface recombination ~10x, so expect 2-5x tail reduction (fact 3).

title: Nanoimprint-printed oxide-TFT access tiers replace EUV economics
idea: IFR: patterning the switch costs nothing. Pattern the access-transistor and wordline levels of BEOL oxide-TFT 1T1C tiers with jet-and-flash nanoimprint (sub-15 nm half-pitch, ~1/10 the per-layer cost, no EUV), using self-aligned double imprint for the densest level, and stack ten tiers.
why: Constraint: EUV and depreciation are ~55% of cost (fact 4); if a tier costs ~1/10 of an EUV front-end layer set, ten tiers fit in today's wafer cost for 10x bits, and the single EUV supplier chokepoint is avoided.

title: Tunnel-diode latch pair inside a one-transistor cell
idea: Two series resonant or Si/SiGe interband tunnel diodes on the storage node (a Goto pair, after TI's late-1990s TSRAM) create two stable voltages held by picoamp current. Access uses a standard DRAM transistor.
why: Refresh-free at near-1T1C area, since the diodes stack vertically, costing ~1 mW per Gb of holding power.

title: Cardiac-pacemaker coupled oscillators sweep refresh as traveling waves
idea: Sinoatrial cells are weakly coupled oscillators with built-in backups; give each subarray a local ring-oscillator refresh timer coupled to its neighbors so the phases lock into a traveling wave, letting refresh march subarray by subarray while the others keep serving.
why: Turns all-bank refresh blackouts (tRFC ~300-500 ns at 32 Gb+) into hidden subarray-level refresh, recovers most of the 10-20% bandwidth, and flattens peak current so pumps can be smaller.

title: Cargo load-planning: per-row data masks keep weak cells discharged
idea: Adapted from ship load planning, which puts heavy cargo where the hull is strongest: using a factory map of weak-retention cells, every write picks one of four XOR scrambling masks (2 tag bits per row) so known weak cells hold the value their leakage pulls them toward. A cell already at its leakage endpoint cannot lose data.
why: Retention failures only hit cells holding the 'uphill' value; steering weak cells to safe values lets each row refresh at the rate of its strong cells, removing the tail from the refresh budget and cutting refresh 4x or more (fact 3) for ~0.4% tag overhead.

title: Refresh may consume no fresh charge: adiabatic bitline recycling between subarrays
idea: Limit: every refresh must reuse the charge of the previous one. Pair subarrays through transfer switches. After subarray A restores, its full-swing bitlines step their charge adiabatically into subarray B's bitlines, which are being precharged, instead of dumping it to ground. This charge seesaw leaves the sense amps only the difference to top up.
why: Fact 3: bitline swing dominates refresh energy. Recycling ~50-60% of it cuts refresh from ~46 fJ/bit toward ~20 fJ/bit with no change to the cell.

title: Eliminate ground dumping: resonant LC adiabatic bitline refresh
idea: During refresh, drive bitline restore from an on-package resonant LC tank (thin-film inductors in the interposer) so charge sloshes between banks instead of being dumped to ground; sense amplifiers only steer the resonant swing. Roughly 60-80% of bitline CV^2 is recovered each refresh cycle.
why: Refresh energy ~46 fJ/bit could drop to ~10-20 fJ/bit, attacking the CV^2 floor (fact 10) without changing the cell.

title: Refresh that gives energy back: resonant bitline charge recycling
idea: Inverts 'refresh charge is dumped to ground': during refresh bursts, bitline pairs swing through an on-die LC tank (an integrated inductor shared per bank) so the energy of charging bitlines is stored magnetically and returned on the next row, approximating adiabatic charging; random accesses keep conventional sensing.
why: Cuts the ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy (fact 3) by ~3-5x and sidesteps the CV2 floor (fact 10) for the refresh share of DRAM power.

title: Substitute biased well with buried fixed-charge Al2O3 back-gate
idea: Substitute the charge-pumped negative body bias (VBB) with a 3-5 nm ALD Al2O3/SiO2 liner on the back side of each buried or vertical channel. Its built-in negative fixed charge (~-5e12 cm^-2) permanently depletes the body near the storage junction and raises off-state Vt by ~150-250 mV at zero standby power.
why: Leakage + periphery: ~10-30x lower subthreshold leakage for tail cells, and the VBB pump and its idle power (part of the 16-33% idle budget) go away.

title: Thin p-epi on p+ substrate with buried sink drains leakage
idea: Fuse the CCD vertical-overflow-drain design with DRAM. Storage nodes sit in thin, lightly doped epi over a heavily doped, short-lifetime substrate, plus an n-buried layer biased as a carrier sink that removes thermally generated charge before it reaches storage nodes.
why: The diffusion leakage component, which dominates at 85 C, falls ~10x, giving 3-5x hot retention.

title: Hole quantum-well floating body in SiGe for long retention
idea: Po: the stored charge lives in a room with no exit. Build a capacitorless floating-body cell with a buried compressively strained SiGe layer under the channel whose valence-band offset traps holes in a quantum well, so stored holes cannot recombine through the source/drain junctions as fast as in plain silicon.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor (4F^2 possible) while band confinement lifts floating-body retention from ~10 ms toward >1 s, cutting refresh 50-100x.

title: Rescue scrapped dies with per-row refresh maps sold as SKU
idea: Po: the trash bin is a warehouse. Dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen because a few hundred rows are weak get a per-row refresh-class map burned into on-die fuses; the module controller refreshes those rows at 16-32 ms and the rest normally, and the parts ship as a mapped-refresh grade.
why: Usable supply: recovering 3-8% of output lost to retention fallout adds bits with no new fab, at <1% bandwidth cost.

title: Heavy-water reactor engineer: deuterium-cured access transistor interfaces
idea: A CANDU operator has tonnes of heavy water on hand. Replace the final forming-gas anneal with a 10-20 atm deuterium anneal so Si/SiO2 and junction dangling bonds are capped with Si-D bonds, which resist hot-carrier and thermal depassivation ~10x better than Si-H and so stop traps from growing into variable-retention cells over life.
why: Narrows the end-of-life leakage tail, letting refresh intervals relax ~1.5-3x and improving yield; deuterium comes from Canada and the U.S., not a chokepoint.

title: Endosymbiotic DRAM layer grown directly on accelerator logic
idea: Mitochondria live inside the host cell instead of in a separate organ; because <=400 C oxide access devices retain charge for seconds even at 85-105 C, fabricate a 1T1C memory layer in the BEOL directly above accelerator compute tiles, wired by vias instead of HBM PHYs and TSVs.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax and most data-movement energy (3-4 pJ/bit to <0.5 pJ/bit), and retention stays usable at logic hot-spot temperatures where silicon DRAM would need 4x refresh.

title: Cross-gated 2T1C: select one cell, not a whole row
idea: Rearrange selection from row-wide to cross-point: in a retired 2x/3x nm DRAM line, give each cell two series access transistors, one on the row wordline and one on a column-select line, so only the cell at the crossing connects. In hold, leakage must cross two off devices in series, and opening a row no longer disturbs its unselected cells.
why: Leakage ~10x lower via stack effect (fact 3), half-select and row-hammer disturbance largely gone (fact 9), 128x page overfetch removed (fact 8); ~1.5-2x density loss is paid in old fabs with spare capacity.

title: Joule self-anneal pulses heal leaky tail cells in the field
idea: Worse: ship cells whose leakage tail is frozen in by process traps forever. Flip: find tail cells with in-DRAM retention tests, then drive a microsecond high-current pulse through that wordline segment to self-heat it locally to ~400 C and anneal the responsible interface traps.
why: Shifts the <=13 fA tail (fact 3) about 2x tighter and recovers yield otherwise lost to retention.

title: Crucible-free float-zone wafers: long carrier lifetime, no quartz crucibles
idea: Revive float-zone crystal growth, sidelined for CMOS by Czochralski: grow nitrogen-doped 200-300 mm FZ silicon in U.S. plants, so storage-node junctions sit in oxygen-free, long-lifetime silicon where generation leakage (proportional to 1/lifetime) is lower. No high-purity quartz crucible is consumed.
why: Lowers storage-node junction generation leakage 2-5x (fact 3) and removes the Spruce Pine HPQ crucible chokepoint (resources).

title: Shared physics-of-failure qualification fast-tracks new hot access devices
idea: Worse: make every new access-device material wait 3 years of 125 C HTOL before anyone buys it. Flip: fund a consortium test house with standardized 200 C accelerated stress and model-based 10-year extrapolation so wide-gap and novel access devices qualify in ~9 months.
why: Cuts time-to-market for low-leakage devices (fact 3) and lowers U.S. entrant barriers.
